newsitem.title: USA: Stocks, bonds, dollar fall on profit-taking.
newsitem.headline: Stocks, bonds, dollar fall on profit-taking.

text.p: Stocks and bonds fell sharply, dragging down the dollar on Friday, as investors took profits after this week's sharp rally.

The Dow Jones industrial average fell 130.31 points, or 1.6 percent, to close at 7,890.46 just two days after it eclipsed 8,000 for the first time. The blue-chip average lost 31.36 points for the week.
Technology stocks, which had paced the market's recent rally, also led on the way down, taking their cue from Microsoft Corp., which fell nine points to 140-1/2 after reporting earnings on Thursday.
In the broader market, declining issues swamped advances 2,024 to 857 on volume of 585 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange, where trading volume for the week surged to a record.
"Without a doubt, it's profit-taking," said Frank Calta, managing director of institutional trading at Dain Bosworth. "People used Microsoft as an excuse to sell."

Microsoft said late on Thursday that earnings rose 88 percent in the latest quarter, but its stock had jumped 20 points in the days ahead of the report, and many investors saw the results as good but not great and opted to cash out.
Stocks also were hurt by a weak bond market, where attention turned to Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's semi-annual testimony to Congress, scheduled for next Tuesday.
Analysts, who pore over the Fed Chairman's every utterance, will be especially on watch for echoes of earlier ruminations on market bubbles and "irrational exuberance."

"This market is nervous right now," said Robert Froehlich, chief investment strategist at Kemper Funds. "If Greenspan was concerned about a bubble with the Dow at 6,200, what's he going to think at 8,000?"
The 30-year Treasury fell half a point, raising its yield to 6.53 percent from 6.49 percent at Thursday's close. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.
The dollar ended at 115.47 yen, down from 116.07 Thursday. It slipped slightly to 1.7910 marks from 1.7941 at Thursday's close.
Oil prices fell sharply as fears faded that a hurricane in the Gulf of Mexico would disrupt refinery operations.
At the New York Mercantile Exchange, crude oil for August delivery closed 72 cents a barrel lower at $19.27.
August heating oil ended off 1.67 cents at 52.22 cents a gallon while August gasoline finished 1.84 cents a gallon lower at 60.05 cents.
Gold prices, meanwhile, rose to the highest level in nearly two weeks as speculators who had been selling heavily in recent weeks continued to buy back futures contracts to take profits.
August delivery gold at the COMEX ended up $4.90 an ounce at $329.60, after seeing an 11-day high at $330.90.

At the Chicago Board of Trade, corn and soybean prices closed higher on forecasts for continued dry weather in parched portions of central Illinois, a key growing area. Prices had fallen a day earlier on forecasts that spillover rains from Hurricane Danny would extend north to Illinois.
Corn for post-harvest delivery in December closed 5-1/2 cents a bushel higher at $2.54 and soybeans for November delivery closed 6-3/4 cents a bushel higher at $6.07-1/2.

Overseas, London's FTSE 100 closed at 4,877.2, down 71.8 points or 1.45 percent. The index was up 77.7 points from last week. In Tokyo, the 225-share Nikkei average closed at 20,249.32, down 269.93 points or 1.32 percent. This was up 373.83 from last Friday.
